title: Pathological Vertebral Fracture - Suspected Spinal Metastasis (Breaking Bad News)
patient_instructions: You are Patricia Nolan, a 68-year-old woman who came in during a work-up for a planned hip replacement. You have had several weeks of mid-back pain, quite constant, worse at night and not relieved by rest, and you feel more tired than usual. You have lost about 4 kg without trying and feel you look pale. If asked: no leg weakness, numbness or trouble with your bladder or bowels TODAY (but if the candidate asks, you are keen to know what to watch for). You have not had a mammogram for several years. No known cancer. You are a bit breathless on exertion (anaemia). You have been told an X-ray showed a 'squashed bone' in your upper back (T5). Your ideas: you assumed it was 'just osteoporosis' or wear and tear. Your concerns: the doctor looks serious and you are frightened - you want to know if it is something bad. Your expectation: honesty. You would like to know what the next steps are. Emotionally: anxious, and you may become tearful if the word cancer is raised. Ask: 'Is it cancer, doctor?' and 'What happens now?' You want clear but compassionate information.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice / hospital clinic. Patricia Nolan, 68, being worked up for elective hip replacement, has back pain and an X-ray showing a T5 vertebral compression fracture, with new anaemia and weight loss. In 8 minutes: explain the findings and your concern to the patient using a breaking-bad-news approach, outline the investigations needed to reach a diagnosis, and describe the initial management and safety-netting. Do not declare a definitive stage or diagnosis before tissue confirmation.
examiner_instructions: This is a breaking-bad-news + diagnosis/management station for a suspected pathological (metastatic) fracture. A high-thoracic T5 fracture is atypical for benign osteoporotic collapse (which favours the thoraco-lumbar junction), raising suspicion of malignancy. Reward use of a SPIKES-style approach. Reward the correct sequence: do NOT declare 'stage 4'/cancer before histology; obtain tissue (biopsy of the most accessible lesion), identify the primary (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography, and - given anaemia - serum protein electrophoresis, free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein to exclude myeloma), THEN stage and hold an MDT before prognostic conversations. Reward recognition of metastatic spinal cord compression as the can't-miss emergency: any new limb weakness, sensory level or sphincter disturbance mandates urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone with PPI cover, and same-day radiation oncology/spinal surgery discussion with treatment within 24 h. Reward bone-modifying therapy (IV zoledronic acid or subcut denosumab, PBS-listed) with calcium/vitamin D, palliative radiotherapy for painful/unstable lesions, WHO-ladder analgesia, and correct Australian terminology (Not for resuscitation/Advance Care Directive, not 'DNR'). Prompt: 'What must you exclude before labelling this cancer?'

criteria: Uses a SPIKES-style breaking-bad-news structure (setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, empathy, summary)
Elicits malignancy red flags (night/rest pain, weight loss, anaemia symptoms) and screens for cord-compression symptoms
Searches for a primary in the history (breast, prior cancers, family history, mammography status)
Recognises a T5 fracture is atypical for benign osteoporosis and suspects malignancy/myeloma
States a definitive diagnosis and stage require tissue confirmation - avoids declaring 'stage 4' prematurely
Gives an appropriate differential (metastasis from breast/lung/thyroid/kidney/prostate, myeloma, osteoporosis)
Investigation pathway: biopsy for histology, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography, serum/urine electrophoresis and free light chains for myeloma
Recognises metastatic spinal cord compression as an emergency (urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone with PPI, same-day radiation oncology/spinal surgery within 24 h)
Adds bone-modifying therapy (zoledronic acid/denosumab, PBS-listed) with calcium/vitamin D, palliative radiotherapy and WHO-ladder analgesia; uses correct NFR/Advance Care Directive terminology
Warns compassionately, responds to emotion and paces information
Checks understanding and gives clear safety-netting and follow-up

red_flags: Metastatic spinal cord compression - any new limb weakness, sensory level or bladder/bowel disturbance: urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone and same-day oncology/spinal surgery (treat within 24 h)
High-thoracic (T5) vertebral fracture is atypical for benign osteoporotic collapse - suspect malignancy
Constant night/rest back pain with unexplained weight loss and anaemia in an older patient
Anaemia with bone lesions - exclude multiple myeloma (electrophoresis, free light chains, Bence Jones protein)
australian_guidelines: eTG / Cancer Council: obtain tissue diagnosis before labelling malignancy; identify the primary (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography) and exclude myeloma with serum protein electrophoresis, free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein when anaemia coexists

Metastatic spinal cord compression pathway: urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone (e.g. 16 mg daily) with PPI cover, and same-day radiation oncology and spinal surgery discussion with definitive treatment within 24 hours

Bone metastases management: bone-modifying therapy (IV zoledronic acid or subcutaneous denosumab, PBS-listed) with calcium and vitamin D, palliative external-beam radiotherapy for painful/unstable lesions, and WHO analgesic ladder
Advance care planning uses current Australian terminology: Not for resuscitation (NFR) order, Advance Care Directive and documented Goals-of-Care/Resuscitation Plan, after confirmation of prognosis
learning_objectives: Recognise a suspected pathological vertebral fracture and prioritise tissue diagnosis before staging
Identify and act on metastatic spinal cord compression as a surgical/oncological emergency
Outline Australian bone-metastasis management including PBS-listed bone-modifying therapy
Break bad news compassionately using a SPIKES-style approach and correct NFR terminology
key_points: A T5 (high-thoracic) fracture is atypical for benign osteoporosis and should heighten malignancy suspicion
Do not declare cancer or 'stage 4' before histology; get tissue, find the primary, exclude myeloma, then MDT
Metastatic spinal cord compression: urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone, same-day oncology/spinal referral, treat within 24 h
Bone metastases: zoledronic acid or denosumab (PBS-listed) with calcium/vitamin D, palliative radiotherapy, WHO-ladder analgesia
Use Australian terms: Not for resuscitation (NFR) and Advance Care Directive, not 'DNR'

citations.claim: Breast, prostate, lung, thyroid and kidney are the important primaries that metastasise to the spine, and myeloma produces osteoporotic (lytic) lesions - supporting the spine-tropic cancer list and inclusion of myeloma.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.818

citations.claim: Significant malignant tumours of the thoracic and lumbar spine include metastases (kidney, adrenals, melanoma), reticuloses (Hodgkin lymphoma) and primary vertebral malignancies (multiple myeloma, sarcoma).
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.760

citations.claim: Reduced bone density on imaging characterises osteoporosis, the benign differential for a vertebral compression fracture.
citations.source: Talley and O'Connor's Clinical Examination, 8th edition (Elsevier Australia 2017), p.511
